claims.reason: 9.2-9.3 do make sensual desire twofold, internal and external. But the Pali 'ajjhattaṁ kāmacchando / bahiddhā kāmacchando' has no 'dhammesu' (unlike doubt at 9.10), so it reads as internal/external sensual desire. 'For what is internal' takes the translator's object reading and turns it into the names of the parts.
Same as dv-01. 9.4 'ajjhattaṁ byāpādo / bahiddhā byāpādo' is internal/external ill will. 'Ill will for what is internal' leans on the English object reading, which the Pali doesn't specify.
9.6-9.7: thinaṁ (dullness) and middhaṁ (drowsiness) are each a hindrance, so the compound hindrance becomes twofold.
9.8-9.9: uddhaccaṁ and kukkuccaṁ are each a hindrance.
9.10-9.11: ajjhattaṁ/bahiddhā dhammesu vicikicchā, which is doubt about internal and external things.
10.2-10.3: ajjhattaṁ/bahiddhā dhammesu sati, each the awakening factor of mindfulness.
11.1-11.2 say this exactly, for internal and external things.
12.1-12.2: kāyikaṁ and cetasikaṁ vīriyaṁ.
13.1-13.2: savitakkasavicārā and avitakkaavicārā pīti.
14.1-14.2: kāyappassaddhi and cittappassaddhi.
15.1-15.2: samādhi with and without vitakka-vicāra.
16.1-16.2: ajjhattaṁ/bahiddhā dhammesu upekkhā.

texts.notes: Twelve divisions (5 + 7) match 9.12 and 16.3. The left-out note is right that 3.2/3.4/6.1/6.3 are the wanderers' words. Only sensual desire and ill will lack 'dhammesu' in the Pali, so only their part names over-read the English.

claims.reason: The English at 1.3 names all seven. The Pali gives the first and last with …pe…, a standard abbreviation of the list.
1.1 and 1.4: developed and cultivated, the seven factors 'apārā pāraṁ gamanāya saṁvattanti'.

texts.notes: The verses (2.1-6.6) are the Buddha's teaching, but the left-out note mentions them, so they are not an unmentioned omission.

claims.reason: The count and members match 1.2-1.5. But the Pali names at 1.4 are 'rūparāgo, arūparāgo' (desire for form / formless). 'Desire for rebirth in the realm of luminous form' imports 'rebirth' and 'luminous' from the English; the Pali doesn't have them.
1.11: nibbānaninnaṁ nibbānapoṇaṁ nibbānapabbhāraṁ. 'Leads to extinguishment' is the rubric's own example of a fair simplification.

1.6/1.12 are a purpose clause: the factors 'should be developed (bhāvetabbā) for' the direct knowledge, complete understanding, finishing and giving up of the fetters. The claim recasts this as an effect, 'leads to giving up', and narrows four aims to one (the wording field keeps all four).
1.9: rāga/dosa/mohavinayapariyosānaṁ.
1.10: amatogadhaṁ amataparāyanaṁ amatapariyosānaṁ.

omissions.what: The first formula variant, in the Pali but dropped from the English: each factor 'vivekanissitaṁ virāganissitaṁ nirodhanissitaṁ vossaggapariṇāmiṁ' (relying on seclusion, fading away, cessation, ripening as letting go). The 'encoded' note lists the variants at 1.9-1.11 only.
The seven awakening factors are enumerated here, but no list claim cites this text.

texts.notes: Marked 'fully encoded' with nothing left out, but the seclusion/letting-go variant at 1.8 is neither encoded nor mentioned. It is easy to miss because Sujato's English for 1.8 omits it.

claims.reason: The members are right, but the citation is incomplete. Pali 1.3 names only kāmacchanda; the other four are at 1.4-1.7, which aren't cited.

1.1/1.8: anibbānasaṁvattanikā.
2.1/2.4: paññābuddhiyā, which means they grow wisdom.
2.1/2.4: nibbānasaṁvattanikā.
